messages.subject: suspicious additional QTL
messages.subject_clean: suspicious additional QTL
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I recently encountered something strange. I have two families that were both derived from the same NIL. When I made linkage maps and ran QTL mapping for each family, I got a corroborating QTL in the two families in the MQM. This QTL is also indicated by one QTL scan in both families. I then integrated the maps of the two families and ran QTL mapping using the combined data from both families. I used family as a covariate. In the combined family mapping, the original QTL is still there, but I'm also getting a second QTL within 10 cM from the original QTL. This second QTL had even higher LOD score than the original QTL (while the LOD for the original QTL decreased substantially) and it took >50% of the phenotypic effect away. On the surface, it seems like a case where a larger sample size allowed us to split a QTL. But several signs suggest that the new QTL is suspicious.

First, to explore the source of the second QTL, I ran QTL mapping on the integrated map in each family separately. In family 1, I'm stilling getting just the original QTL. The map of family 1 include markers associated with both the original and the new QTL. In family 2, I got the new QTL on the integrated map. But the linkage map of this family does not include markers associated with the new QTL (they were filtered out by segregation distortion). In other words, in family 2, using genotypes at additional markers on the integrated map that were not segregating according to the expected ratio, I'm getting an additional (and even more significant) QTL, which is counterintuitive as the genotype segregation pattern and the phenotype variation do not match well in this part of the map for family 2.

Of course just due to random chance, the phenotypic distribution is somewhat biased towards the right end. It is therefore likely that markers that do not fit the expected segregation ratio may actually fit better. However, I compared the genotype distribution at markers under the original and the new QTL, and the distribution at the original marker fits better with the phenotypic distribution.

Second, family 1 map contains the region associated with the new QTL but there is no evidence of a QTL in that region.

The two QTL has the same sign so they are not artificial QTL in repulsion. I am suspicious about the new QTL. I'm wondering if you have any suggestions on what else I should check to tell whether the new QTL is an artifact or not.

Many thanks and sorry for the long, complicated post.

Mingzi

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Warning message: Strange genotype pattern.
messages.body_plain:
Hello Karl

Sorry if this question seems dumb to you. I have a genetic map who is supposed to be from a backcross.
The map has A, B, H, 0 and read.cross reads is as F2.
Is there a problem with the coding or should I read the cross differently

Thanks

L

On Thursday, 3 August 2017 18:52:39 UTC+1, Karl Broman wrote:

> If read.cross sees genotypes that are just AA and AB, it assumes that it's a backcross.
> If it sees any BB genotypes, it assumes it's an intercross.
>
> I'm not quite sure how you want the data to be treated.
>
> karl
>
>
> > On Aug 3, 2017, at 12:22 PM, joa...@gmx.com wrote:
> >
> > I'm working with a family of offspring from two wild parents, and as I didn't have phase information or genetic distances (only physical), I have used the LinkMFEX package. This analyses the male and female mapping parent separately to calculate map distances, and gives most probable phase for each linkage group, with alleles coded as A or H for the female parent data set and B or H for the male parent.
> >
> > Now when I enter these into R/qtl, the female data set is interpreted as a backcross
> >  (Genotypes (%):      AA:55.0  AB:45.0)
> > and the male set as an F2 intercross
> >  (Genotypes (%):      AA:0.0  AB:43.1  BB:56.9  not BB:0.0  not AA:0.0)
> > with the message (for the male only): strange genotype pattern.
> >
> > So is this allele coding not correctly interpreted by R/qtl? And why might the two data sets (from the same offspring) behave differently? Thanks for any advice!
> >

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Warning message: Strange genotype pattern.
messages.body_plain:
If it's a backcross, there should just be two possible genotypes, say A:H or H:B.
If there are just a few A's (or B's), you could use genotypes=c("A","H") or genotypes=c("B", "H") in read.cross() and have the other homozygote treated as missing.

karl

I am confused about the number of markers to analysis. I have 180 individuals with around 600,000 SNPs and have constructed a genetic map based on them. These SNPs were retained by a set of data cleaning processed. The genetic map consists of 5000 unique loci with all these SNPs where some SNPs located in the same place in a linkage group.

Now  I'm not sure whether it is necessary to conduct QTL mapping with such a large number of markers. Is this just a time-consuming program if all markers are kept? If there is no need to analyse this with so much data, how should I filter markers?

Thanks,

Syue

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] the Number of Markers for QTL
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] the Number of Markers for QTL
messages.body_plain:
It depends on the type of cross and the size of the genome. In recombinant inbred lines or an advanced intercross population, it could be good to have very dense markers. But in a backcross or intercross, there's not much value in having markers that are <1 cM apart.

I would start with findDupMarkers() and cut down on markers that have identical data.
There's also pickMarkerSubset() which picks out a set of markers with no two markers closer than some chosen distance.

karl

messages.subject: Multiple QTL model analysis with covariate
messages.subject_clean: Multiple QTL model analysis with covariate
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

Currently, I am performing a QTL analysis with a RIL population (F6)  in R/QTL.
I have identified a covariate which affects the phenotype I use for the mapping, and and using the scanone analysis I have determined that this is most likely an additive covariate.

Now I want to use this information in the Multiple QTL model I am building with the fitqtl and refineqtl options. I was wondering: Do I then add these covariates to the model as follows y~Q1+Q2+Q1*Q1+Covariate,  or do I need to put the model as Q1+Q2+Q1*Q2+  Q1 + Covariate + Q2 + Covariate ?

Also I was thinking,  is it wise to again test here whether I have an additive or interacting covariate? (e.g. adding the covariate as an additive and as interacting covariate to the multiple QTL model, and then compare which model has the best LOD-scores?)

Thanks!

Best Wishes,
Jasper

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Multiple QTL model analysis with covariate
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Multiple QTL model analysis with covariate
messages.body_plain:
In the fitqtl/refineqtl functions, you need to create a data frame of
covariates, and you refer to the individual columns by their column names.

If an additive covariate, you'd just write like

   y ~ Q1+Q2+Q1*Q2+Covariate

If you want to include an interaction with QTL 1, you'd do

   y ~ Q1+Q2+Q1*Q2+Covariate + Covariate:Q1

: is for a specific interaction
* includes the interaction plus all marginal effects

Yes I would reevaluate the evidence for the QTL and interactions in the
context of the multiple-QTL model.

karl

messages.body_plain:
I don't fully understand. If you're trying to establish the significance
of QTL pairs/interactions, you need to look at scantwo permutations, not
scanone permutations.

If you're not looking for QTL x covariate interactions, but just want to
include the covariate as an additive term in all models, you'd include
it as an additive covariate in each of scanone and scantwo, and the
permutations for them.

In general, I'd trust the multiple-QTL model over the results of scantwo.

karl
